notes:
Rutherford's Model

  • Alpha-particle scattering: most alpha particles pass straight through; a few are deflected at large angles (some >90°) — showed that atom has a tiny, massive, positively charged nucleus with electrons orbiting it, mostly empty space.
  • Distance of closest approach: $r_0 = \dfrac{2kZe^2}{E_k}$ (head-on collision), where $E_k$ is the KE of the alpha particle.
  • Drawback: could not explain stability of atom (accelerating electron should radiate energy and spiral into nucleus) or line spectra.

Bohr's Model (for hydrogen-like atoms)

  • Postulates: electrons revolve in stationary orbits without radiating; angular momentum is quantised, $L = mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$; radiation emitted/absorbed only when electron jumps orbits, $h\nu = E_i - E_f$.
  • Radius: $r_n = \dfrac{n^2h^2\varepsilon_0}{\pi mZe^2} \propto \dfrac{n^2}{Z}$; for hydrogen $r_n = 0.529n^2$ Å.
  • Energy: $E_n = -\dfrac{13.6Z^2}{n^2}$ eV (for hydrogen, $Z=1$). Ground state energy $=-13.6$ eV; ionisation energy from ground state $=13.6$ eV.
  • Speed: $v_n \propto Z/n$. For hydrogen, $v_1 = 2.18\times10^6$ m/s.

Hydrogen Spectrum

  • $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = RZ^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2}-\dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$, $R = 1.097\times10^7\ \text{m}^{-1}$ (Rydberg constant).
SeriesFinal level $n_1$Region
Lyman1Ultraviolet
Balmer2Visible
Paschen3Infrared
Brackett4Infrared
Pfund5Infrared
  • Maximum number of spectral lines from level $n$ to lower levels $= \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$.
  • Total energy $E_n$ is negative (bound system); $KE = -E_n$ (magnitude), $PE = 2E_n$, by the virial theorem for Coulomb force.

    • Exam tip

    KCET typically asks 2 questions: one on Bohr energy/radius/wavelength formulas (numerical) and one conceptual on Rutherford scattering or spectral series identification.

questions.q: In Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment, the observation that a few alpha particles bounced back at angles greater than 90° indicated that
options: the atom is mostly empty space
electrons are located inside the nucleus
the positive charge and mass of the atom are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
questions.explanation: Large-angle scattering requires a strong repulsive force from a concentrated positive charge; this could only happen if nearly all the mass and positive charge occupy a very small volume (the nucleus).
questions.trick: Large-angle bounce-back needs a tiny, massive, charged nucleus doing the repelling.

questions.q: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is 0.529 Å. The radius of the second orbit is
questions.trick: $r_n\propto n^2$ — square the orbit number, multiply by $r_1$.

questions.q: The energy of the electron in the ground state of hydrogen is $-13.6$ eV. Its energy in the first excited state ($n=2$) is
questions.trick: $E_n=-13.6/n^2$ eV — just square $n$ and divide.

questions.q: The ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state is
questions.explanation: Ionisation energy = energy needed to take the electron from $n=1$ ($E_1=-13.6$ eV) to $n=\infty$ ($E_\infty = 0$), i.e. 13.6 eV.
questions.trick: Ionisation energy from the ground state is always $13.6$ eV — memorise it.

questions.q: In the Bohr model, the angular momentum of an electron in the $n$th orbit is quantised as
questions.explanation: Bohr's quantisation postulate: $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, $n = 1,2,3,\dots$.
questions.trick: Bohr quantisation: $L=nh/2\pi$ — the one formula behind everything else.

questions.q: An electron in a hydrogen atom transitions from $n=3$ to $n=1$. This transition belongs to the
questions.explanation: Transitions ending at $n_1 = 1$ constitute the Lyman series, which lies in the ultraviolet region.
questions.trick: Ends at $n=1$ is Lyman; $n=2$ is Balmer; $n=3$ is Paschen — memorise the ladder.

questions.q: The maximum number of spectral lines emitted when an electron in a hydrogen atom de-excites from $n = 4$ to lower levels is
questions.explanation: Number of lines $= \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = \dfrac{4\times3}{2} = 6$.
questions.trick: Max spectral lines from level $n$: $n(n-1)/2$ — a combinatorics shortcut.

questions.q: The speed of an electron in the $n$th Bohr orbit of hydrogen varies as
questions.explanation: From Bohr's theory, $v_n = \dfrac{Ze^2}{2\varepsilon_0 nh} \propto Z/n$; for hydrogen ($Z=1$), $v_n \propto 1/n$.
questions.trick: $v_n\propto Z/n$; for hydrogen it's just $v_n\propto1/n$.

questions.q: The wavelength of the first line of the Balmer series (transition $n=3 \to n=2$) in hydrogen is close to (use $R = 1.097\times10^7\ \text{m}^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{9}\right) = R\times\dfrac{5}{36} = 1.097\times10^7\times0.1389 \approx 1.524\times10^6\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda \approx 656$ nm (H-alpha line).
questions.trick: Balmer 656 nm (H-alpha) is the classic $3\to2$ transition, worth memorising directly.

questions.q: According to Bohr's model, the total energy of an electron in a stationary orbit is
options: always negative, indicating a bound system
questions.explanation: $E_n = -13.6Z^2/n^2$ eV is negative for every orbit, showing the electron is bound to the nucleus; energy becomes zero only when $n\to\infty$ (free electron).
questions.trick: $E_n$ is always negative — that just means the electron is bound, not free.

questions.q: In a hydrogen-like atom, the potential energy and kinetic energy of the electron in an orbit are related by
questions.explanation: For an inverse-square (Coulomb) force, the virial theorem gives $PE = -2KE$, and total energy $E = KE + PE = -KE$, consistent with $E_n$ being negative.
questions.trick: Virial theorem for the Coulomb force: $PE=-2KE$, so $E=KE+PE=-KE$.

questions.q: The shortest wavelength in the Lyman series of hydrogen corresponds to a transition from
questions.explanation: Shortest wavelength (highest energy, series limit) corresponds to the largest possible energy gap, i.e. from $n=\infty$ down to $n=1$.
questions.trick: Series limit (shortest $\lambda$) always means the biggest possible jump: from $n=\infty$.

questions.q: A hydrogen atom is excited from its ground state to $n=3$. The number of possible wavelengths that can be emitted as it returns to the ground state is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = \dfrac{3\times2}{2} = 3$ possible transitions/wavelengths: $3\to2$, $2\to1$, $3\to1$.
questions.trick: 3 possible transitions from $n=3$ to ground: $3(3-1)/2=3$ — just compute directly.

questions.q: The main drawback of Rutherford's atomic model was that it could not explain
options: the small size of the nucleus
the stability of atoms and the observed discrete line spectra
questions.explanation: Classically, an orbiting (accelerating) electron should continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, making atoms unstable, and the model gave no explanation for the discrete spectral lines observed.
questions.trick: Rutherford's fatal gaps: no atomic stability, no line spectra explanation.

questions.q: For a hydrogen-like ion with $Z = 2$ (singly ionised helium), the ground state energy is
questions.trick: $E_1=-13.6Z^2$ — square $Z$ first, then multiply.

questions.q: An alpha particle with kinetic energy 5 MeV is projected head-on towards a gold nucleus ($Z=79$). Its distance of closest approach is proportional to
questions.explanation: $r_0 = \dfrac{2kZe^2}{E_k}$, so the distance of closest approach is inversely proportional to the kinetic energy of the alpha particle.
questions.trick: Closest approach $r_0\propto1/E_k$ — higher KE means the alpha gets closer.

questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of the electron in the $n$th Bohr orbit is related to the orbit's circumference by
questions.explanation: Bohr's quantisation $mvr = nh/2\pi$ combined with de Broglie's $\lambda = h/mv$ gives $2\pi r_n = n\lambda$ — an integer number of de Broglie wavelengths fit the orbit, providing a physical basis for quantisation.
questions.trick: Bohr plus de Broglie: $2\pi r_n=n\lambda$ — integer wavelengths fit the orbit exactly.

questions.q: The energy released when an electron transitions from $n=2$ to $n=1$ in hydrogen is
questions.explanation: $E_2 - E_1 = (-3.4) - (-13.6) = 10.2$ eV, emitted as a photon (Lyman-alpha line).
questions.trick: The $n=2\to1$ energy gap is the famous $10.2$ eV Lyman-alpha line.

questions.q: The radius of the first Bohr orbit ($n=1$) of a singly ionised helium atom ($Z=2$) is
questions.trick: $r_n\propto n^2/Z$ — divide the hydrogen radius by $Z$ for ions.

questions.q: The frequency of revolution of the electron in the $n$th Bohr orbit of hydrogen varies as
questions.explanation: Since $v_n \propto 1/n$ and $r_n \propto n^2$, the revolution frequency $f = v_n/(2\pi r_n) \propto 1/n^3$.
questions.trick: Revolution frequency $f=v/(2\pi r)\propto1/n^3$ — combine the $v_n$ and $r_n$ laws.

questions.q: The ionisation energy of a doubly ionised lithium atom, Li$^{2+}$ ($Z=3$), in its ground state is
questions.explanation: Ionisation energy $= 13.6Z^2 = 13.6\times9 = 122.4$ eV.
questions.trick: Ionisation energy scales as $13.6Z^2$ eV — just square the atomic number.

questions.q: Which spectral series of hydrogen lies entirely in the infrared region and results from transitions ending at $n=3$?
questions.explanation: Transitions ending at $n_1=3$ constitute the Paschen series, which lies entirely in the infrared region.
questions.trick: Ends at $n=3$ means the Paschen series, always infrared — pair the number with the name.

questions.q: A hydrogen spectral line has wavelength 486 nm, one of the well-known Balmer lines. This corresponds to the transition
questions.explanation: The Balmer line at 486 nm (H-beta) arises from the transition $n=4 \to n=2$.
questions.trick: 486 nm (H-beta) is the specific $4\to2$ Balmer transition — a memorisable pair.

questions.q: The energy required to excite a hydrogen atom from its ground state to the $n=3$ level is approximately
questions.trick: Excitation energy is $E_{final}-E_{initial}$; both negative, so subtract carefully.

questions.q: In Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment, the fact that most alpha particles passed through the gold foil almost undeflected indicates that
options: the nucleus occupies most of the atom's volume
the atom is mostly empty space
questions.explanation: If most alpha particles pass through undeviated, then most of the atom's volume must contain no significant charge or mass, i.e. the atom is mostly empty space, with charge and mass concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
questions.trick: Most alphas pass straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space.

questions.q: The angular momentum of the electron in the third Bohr orbit ($n=3$) of hydrogen is
questions.explanation: By Bohr's quantisation rule, $L = nh/2\pi$; for $n=3$, $L = 3h/2\pi$.
questions.trick: Angular momentum for $n=3$: just plug into $L=nh/2\pi$.

questions.q: The distance of closest approach of an alpha particle to a nucleus is inversely proportional to its kinetic energy $E_k$. If $E_k$ is doubled, the distance of closest approach
questions.explanation: $r_0 = \dfrac{2kZe^2}{E_k} \propto 1/E_k$, so doubling the kinetic energy halves the distance of closest approach.
questions.trick: Doubling KE halves the closest-approach distance ($r_0\propto1/E_k$).

questions.q: The shortest wavelength (series limit) of the Balmer series of hydrogen is approximately (use $R = 1.097\times10^7\ \text{m}^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: Series limit corresponds to $n_2\to\infty$: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-0\right) = R/4 \approx 2.74\times10^6\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda \approx 365$ nm.
questions.trick: Balmer series limit: $1/\lambda=R/4$ — set $n_2\to\infty$, $n_1=2$.

questions.q: Bohr's postulate that electrons revolve in certain stable orbits without radiating energy directly contradicts
options: the law of conservation of charge
classical electromagnetic theory, which predicts that an accelerating charge should continuously radiate energy
questions.explanation: Classically, an electron moving in a circular orbit is accelerating and should radiate energy continuously, spiralling into the nucleus; Bohr's postulate of non-radiating stationary orbits was an ad hoc departure from classical theory needed to explain atomic stability.
questions.trick: Bohr's 'no radiation' postulate directly defies classical EM theory — that's the point.

questions.q: A hydrogen atom is excited to the $n=5$ level. The maximum number of different spectral lines it can emit while returning to the ground state is
questions.explanation: Maximum number of spectral lines $= \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = \dfrac{5\times4}{2} = 10$.
questions.trick: $n(n-1)/2$ again: for $n=5$, that's $5\times4/2=10$ lines.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom is INCORRECT?
options: Energy levels get closer together as $n$ increases
Electron orbits are circular and quantised
Angular momentum is quantised in integral multiples of $h/2\pi$
Energy is emitted continuously as the electron revolves in its stationary orbit
questions.explanation: A key Bohr postulate is that electrons do NOT radiate energy while in a stationary orbit; energy is emitted only during a transition between orbits, so the statement of continuous emission is incorrect.
questions.trick: Trap: Bohr orbits do NOT emit continuously — only during a jump between orbits.

questions.q: In a hydrogen atom, an electron makes a transition from $n=4$ ($E_4 = -0.85$ eV) to $n=1$ ($E_1 = -13.6$ eV). The frequency of the emitted photon is approximately
questions.trick: Photon frequency: find $\Delta E$ in joules, then $\nu=\Delta E/h$.

questions.q: The Bohr model successfully explains the observed line spectrum of
options: hydrogen and other single-electron (hydrogen-like) ions only
questions.explanation: Bohr's model, based on a single electron orbiting a nucleus, accurately predicts the spectra of hydrogen and hydrogen-like ions (He$^+$, Li$^{2+}$, etc.) but fails for multi-electron atoms due to electron-electron interactions.
questions.trick: Bohr's model only works for single-electron systems — fails for multi-electron atoms.

questions.q: For a hydrogen-like atom, the kinetic energy of the electron in the $n$th orbit is related to its total energy $E_n$ by
questions.explanation: By the virial theorem for a Coulomb (inverse-square) force, $PE = -2KE$ and $E_n = KE+PE = -KE$, so $KE = -E_n$.
questions.trick: $KE=-E_n$ always — kinetic energy is just minus the (negative) total energy.

questions.q: The energy of the photon emitted during the transition $n=2 \to n=1$ in a singly ionised helium atom (Z=2) is
questions.trick: For ions, compute $E_n=-13.6Z^2/n^2$ first, then subtract for $\Delta E$.

questions.q: As the principal quantum number $n$ increases in the Bohr model of hydrogen, successive energy levels become
questions.explanation: Since $E_n \propto -1/n^2$, the spacing between consecutive levels, $E_{n+1}-E_n$, decreases as $n$ increases, so the levels crowd closer together near $E=0$.
questions.trick: Levels crowd closer as $n$ grows — spacing shrinks like differences of $1/n^2$.

questions.q: The observation of discrete (line) spectra emitted by atoms, rather than a continuous spectrum, is direct evidence for
options: quantisation of energy levels in atoms
the purely wave nature of electrons
a continuous distribution of atomic energy
the existence of neutrons in the nucleus
questions.explanation: Only discrete, quantised energy levels can produce sharp spectral lines at specific frequencies corresponding to specific energy differences, as opposed to a continuous spread of frequencies.
questions.trick: Discrete spectral lines are direct proof energy levels are quantised, not continuous.

questions.q: An electron in a hydrogen atom has total energy $-0.85$ eV. The value of the principal quantum number $n$ for this state is
questions.trick: Given $E_n$, solve $n^2=13.6/|E_n|$ to find the quantum number.

questions.q: For hydrogen-like atoms, the wavelength of the radiation emitted for a transition between two fixed energy levels varies with the atomic number $Z$ as
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} \propto Z^2$ for fixed $n_1, n_2$, so $\lambda \propto 1/Z^2$.
questions.trick: Fixed transition, varying $Z$: wavelength scales as $1/Z^2$.

questions.q: Which of the following series-region pairings is INCORRECTLY matched?
questions.explanation: The Balmer series lies in the visible region, not the ultraviolet; only the Lyman series lies in the ultraviolet, so 'Balmer – Ultraviolet' is the incorrect pairing.
questions.trick: Trap: Balmer is VISIBLE, not ultraviolet — only Lyman lies in UV.
